preface.heading: Why this exists
paragraphs: Most of what harms a group of people is quietly intrusive, arriving as a feeling you cannot place, a conversation that leaves you smaller than it found you, or a process that wears you down. These insidious items are easier to prevent and resist when they have names and definitions.

This glossary is not a list of rules nor offenses; every entry describes something people do, usually people who meant well. Knowing these words can shorten the distance to truth and understanding, and can reduce the amount of suffering of everyone involved when identified and avoided.

preface.heading: How to use it
paragraphs: Start with the section that matches where the pressure seems to be coming from, the name will usually find you.
Every entry is numbered so that a person can say a number out loud and everyone can find it quickly. Here are some cautions before you use it:
list: Naming is not proving, it simply begins a conversation. It is neither verdict nor closure.
Items can be raised against something being required of you by another, or as an acknowledgement of behavior.
Identifying a behavior can begin an AIM: acknowledge (name) what happened, investigate for a set of root causes, then decide if mending behavior or a document is needed so it does not happen again.
Every item in this glossary can be weaponized. Purposeful misuse to inflict harm as cruelty violates our core doctrine.

Items should not be raised as defense against criticism, disagreement, and being told you caused suffering or a harm: these are not demands nor attempts at exploitation. There is a fine line that can exist within a single sentence; we need to remain mindful of what is a point of view and what is an intended manipulation. One is autonomy, the other is subversion.

If mistakes are made, they belong to the person who made them to do with as they please. Mistakes are powerful learning tools and bring wisdom. Denying your mistakes is an act of shunning knowledge that was paid for. Owning mistakes is healthy and causes less suffering.

sections.title: Section One. What can happen inside a person
sections.summary: These need no one else present. They run on their own once they start, and they are often mistaken for personal failings.

entries.text: After enough situations happen that cannot be changed, a person can stop trying even once things can be changed. Newer research says the giving up is the default, and it is having control that has to be learned. The way out is not encouragement. It is small real choices that actually work, made over and over.

The private rule that saying what is needed will cost the relationship, which makes a person stop saying what they need. Holding a boundary quietly is not the same thing. The difference is whether the boundary and the cost is known or assumed.
The harder something was to join, the more it is valued afterward. This is why demanding entry processes create loyal members. The loyalty is real, but also manufactured.
The years already spent become the reason to spend more.
Good already done becomes quiet permission for harm. It sounds like: we are the good ones, so this is different when we do it.
Treating suffering as proof that someone deserved it. Turned inward it becomes the belief that what happened was owed.
Deciding that what is done settles the future in stone.

sections.title: Section Two. What happens between two people
sections.summary: These need one other person, usually one who is depend on or trusted. Dependence and confusion makes them work.

entries.text: Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender. When confronted, a person denies the behavior, attacks the credibility of the person confronting them, and then flips the roles so they are the wronged party and the victim is now the offender. Research finds that being on the receiving end of this increases self-blame.
Not seeing a betrayal because seeing it would cost something that is believed to be of greater value.

Warmth and coldness given unpredictably. This produces stronger attachment than steady kindness does, and it is much harder to walk away from. It requires no beliefs and no doctrine. It is just a pattern.
Being made to doubt what is seen, heard, or felt; attacks on perception itself.
A small request agreed to first, then a larger one, then a larger one. Each step looks reasonable next to the step before. The distance is only visible from the start.
Being worked on until remorse is performed. It ends when the performance is convincing, which means nothing gets fixed.
Making one person the cause of something a system produced. Blame ends the search.
Being expected to disclose faults, doubts, or history, to a person or to a group with no protections. It turns into performance, and heavy confessors gain the standing to judge others.

sections.title: Section Three. What a group does with nobody leading it
sections.summary: These need only a crowd. No leader gives the order and often no one intends it.

entries.text: Most people privately disagree, each one believes they are alone, and the silence keeps a position alive that almost nobody actually holds. This is why anonymous ways of answering can matter more than open ones.
The more people who see a problem, the less likely any one of them acts. Everyone assumes someone else will. A duty that belongs to everyone belongs to no one.

Going over the same distress together, again and again. It makes people closer and it makes them worse at the same time. A group built to support people will produce this by accident unless they watch for it.
The line between a person and the group dissolves, so a threat to the group feels like a threat to your body. It predicts extreme action on the group's behalf better than ordinary belonging does.

Group condemnation of a member that arises organically. It spreads by contamination: supporting the target is suspicious, so friends peel away one at a time. It works through trust, which means it only works on people who believe in the group.

There is no such thing as a group without structure. Refusing formal structure does not remove leadership, it hides it and makes it unaccountable. A test: are decisions argued out more outside the meeting than inside it? Whose approval has to be checked before something happens? Is it a faction leader or splinter group forming? Power often craves centralization.

Each person takes a slightly stricter position than the last, and holding yesterday's position becomes suspect. Nobody set the standard, so nobody can lower it. Moderating is treated as evidence against someone.
Accusing someone of being a plant or a spy. It cannot be disproved, because denial is exactly what a plant would say.
Disagreeing is made socially expensive, then silence gets counted as agreement. Consensus processes are more open to this than voting, because there is no private moment.
Using a position on some unrelated question as a test of belonging. It is how a group narrows without anyone deciding to narrow it.

sections.title: Section Four. What is done from a position of authority
sections.summary: These need an office, a leader, or someone who claims to speak for something larger. If something is being done and it comes with a title behind it, this might be where to find it.

entries.text: Controlling what people see, hear, read, write, and say, and eventually what they say to themselves. It ends in being cut off from the world outside. Everything else in this section is easier once this is in place.

Replacing thinking with in-group words. Slogans and catchphrases that end a question instead of opening it. This is the earliest sign, because it shows up before anyone means any harm. Test: could a first-time visitor read our documents without a glossary of our own words?
Treating a teaching as final truth that may not be questioned, and treating its authors and its current keepers as beyond criticism.

Arranging an experience and presenting it as something that happened on its own, to prove authority or a special gift. It also excuses lying to outsiders, on the grounds that people outside can be deceived for a higher purpose.
Telling someone that what they experienced is not what they experienced, because the teaching says otherwise. Gaslighting specifically applied to doctrine.
Requiring an answer to a pointed question that fits into a held view of perfection, then using guilt and shame to close the gap. It needs a scale, so anything countable feeds it.
A group claiming the right to say who is a real person, and denying anyone who isn’t declared a real person the right to live as they choose.
Knowledge held back for those who are ready. Any two-level structure of knowing, however kindly it is explained.
A closed text with controlled access. Closing a text does not remove authority. It moves the authority to whoever explains the text, and makes that position more valuable than the text.

A short core document beside a long explanation, where people quote the explanation because that is the part that answers questions. Over time the commentary becomes the scripture and its writers become the authority.
Any requirement to account for what is inside a person’s thoughts. Sincerity checks, loyalty tests, correct belief, purity of intention, purity tests, pledges.
The founder or former officeholder who stays on to advise. Influence without an office, which means no term, no limit, and no way to remove them.
Someone outside, often the press, decides who speaks for us, and the choice becomes true because everyone treats it as true. No internal decision was ever made.
Removal that requires other people to cut contact. The engine is the second rule: anyone who keeps talking to the removed person is removed too. That converts private conscience into enforcement.
A body that absorbs an individual’s other obligations instead of sitting beside them. A belief that replaces family, work, other commitments, or other faiths.

sections.title: Section Five. What is built into how an organization runs
sections.summary: These need no bad actor at all. They live in money, process, buildings, and paperwork, and they can run for years while everyone involved means well. If something is going wrong and you cannot find anyone to blame, it is likely here.

entries.text: A departure from the standard that produces no harm the first time, and so becomes the new standard. Repeated, it moves the line without anyone deciding to move it. What would have been refused all at once is arrived at by steps small enough that none was worth objecting to.

Harm that comes from a body failing to prevent or respond to a wrong done inside it. It makes the original injury worse. The known repair is institutional courage: accountability, transparency, responding well to disclosures, asking anonymously whether people have been harmed, and then acting on the answers.
The same deny, attack, and role reversal done by an organization. The body denies the wrong, questions the motives of whoever raised it, and casts itself as the real victim of a witch hunt.

Once a group has accepted a wrongdoer's version of events, raising the concern again does not get it reconsidered. It gets the person attacked. The group has learned to hear accountability as aggression.

Capture by price rather than by rule. No one takes away the right to go. Leaving is simply made to cost income, housing, family, or a person's whole understanding of the world. Everything else in this section is easier once this is in place.
Aid tied, even gently, to belief, attendance, or membership. Historically the converts were called rice Christians. This is the oldest way religion has ever taken hold of people.
A sacred act with a price on it. It drifts toward fear, because whoever is selling needs the buyer to be afraid.

The standing to say something should be done and the means to do it, held by the same person. Also, the power to say what the doctrine means and the power to control the property, held at the same level. Every religious body that went badly wrong held both.
A council or board that picks its own replacements. Also, the ability of an outside agent to seize power, authority, or both by invoking the organizations own canon.

Combined power granted for a crisis and never given back. Nearly every constitution has this hole and most are eaten through it. An expiry that happens whether or not the trouble is over, and can only be reinstated by a separate entity.

A horizontal distinction hardening into a vertical one. Standing that describes what someone has learned becomes standing that decides what others must do. The signs are a test that is unpublished or moves, a cap on how many may hold it, deference owed to the rank rather than to the argument, and a chain forming where there was a circle.
Good done written down as credit and harm as debt, with someone holding the book.
The only place to complain about a person is that person's office.
Information kept quiet to protect the body. It is always defended as discretion, privacy, or not airing things in public.
Closing windows, final chances, now or never. This is how reasonable people are made to stop thinking.

Control through stamina. Long meetings, important items placed last, endless rounds. Whoever can stay the longest decides, which quietly hands the body to people without jobs, children, illness, or limited energy.
The work drifts toward whatever can be paid for, staff become the people it answers to, and the body turns into an organization rather than what it was.
A real danger from outside used to justify extraordinary measures inside, secrecy first among them. It arrives with a very good reason attached.
A small organized group joining an open one in order to take it over. Open membership and low barriers are exactly what this is aimed at.
A body that needs an enemy to hold together, and therefore cannot afford to win.

sections.title: Section Six. Traps in argument
sections.summary: These are ways of arguing that leave no way to answer well.
intro: These are ways of arguing that leave no good way to answer. Naming one does not win the argument. Every name in this section can also be used to dodge a fair question.

entries.text: Denial is treated as proof. Anyone innocent would not object. No answer is available, which is the point.

A strong contested claim is made, and when it is challenged the speaker retreats to a weaker claim nobody would argue with, then returns to the strong one later. The sign is that the two versions are never said in the same breath.
Explaining why someone believes a thing before showing that it is wrong. It turns a disagreement into a diagnosis.
A saying that closes a question without answering it.
Answering a weaker version of a position than the one actually held, and answering it well. The sign is that the person defending has to spend their turn saying what they did not say.
Narrowing the definition of the group in order to throw out an example that does not fit.
Holding one side to a standard of evidence the other side is not held to. No single request is unreasonable. The pattern is the problem.
Endless polite requests for evidence and clarification, meant to exhaust rather than to learn. Any one exchange looks like good faith.
Suggesting something through a question, so nothing was actually claimed and nothing can be answered.
More assertions than can be answered in the time available. Volume beats accuracy.
Opposition dressed as worry for the other side's success.
A question built so that any answer accepts something never agreed to.
Rejecting a real improvement because it is not a complete solution. This is the purity spiral in the form of an argument.
The standard is met, and a new one is given.
Two options offered as though they were the only two.
A rule that applies to everyone, with an exception carved out for one case and no reason given for the exception.
Discrediting a speaker in advance so that whatever they say next is already suspect.
Answering the speaker instead of the argument. Character may be relevant to trust. It is never relevant to whether a claim is true.
Treating where an idea came from as a verdict on whether it is true. A true thing from a bad source is still true.
Answering a charge by naming someone else's wrong. It may be a fair observation. It is not an answer.

Treating what is natural as what is right. This one is aimed at us in particular. The teaching draws heavily on the natural world, and every one of those is a description rather than an instruction. Nature contains everything, so nature can be made to permit anything.

sections.title: Section Seven. Persuasion and propaganda
sections.summary: These are techniques for moving many people at once. These same tools build culture and shape values, sometimes for good. What separates the two is honesty about what is being done.
intro: These are techniques for moving many people at once. They are used on us from outside and they are available to us from inside, which is why they are here. The same tools build culture and shape values, sometimes for good. What separates the two is honesty about what is being done.

entries.text: Attaching bad names to a group, a belief, an institution, or a person, to create dislike without any examination.

A fine sounding word used to win approval without evidence. Honour, freedom, family, security. Vague enough that everyone hears their own meaning, and always favorable. The tests are what the phrase actually means, whether there is a real connection between the idea and the words, and whether the idea still stands with the fine words removed.
Borrowing the good name of a respected symbol by standing next to it.
An endorsement from someone with no standing to give one.
A speaker performing humble origins to borrow trust.
True things selected and arranged to mislead. Nothing said is false.
A softer word put in place of the true one, so that what is happening becomes harder to see and harder to weigh. Harvesting, processing, letting someone go, enhanced measures.
Everyone is already doing it.

A large number of messages sent fast, constantly, and through many channels at once, with no commitment to being true and no commitment to being consistent. The contradictions are not a mistake. It works partly because things repeated often start to feel true, and because people accept the first believable version they hear. Answering each falsehood does not work against it.
The same overwhelming done with actions and announcements rather than lies. Nothing can be examined because everything is happening at once.
Manufactured support made to look like it arose on its own. It works because a story is believed more readily when it seems to come from several places at once.
A message one audience hears clearly and another cannot, so it can be denied.
A claim too large to be dismissed as a mistake, repeated until arguing with it seems unhinged.

Moving a position by small steps until what was unthinkable is ordinary. Each step is small enough not to be worth objecting to. The window is the range of what can currently be said without penalty, and it can be dragged.
A statement heard many times comes to feel true regardless of evidence. No one has to intend it. It is how memory works.

closing.heading: A last word
paragraphs: Nothing in this glossary is unique to us and nothing in it is new. Every one of these has been done by people who believed they were doing right, in organizations founded by people who meant well.
We will do some of these. The question is not whether we notice, it is whether noticing is safe.

closing.heading: Where these come from
paragraphs: Section Four draws on Robert Jay Lifton, Thought Reform and the Psychology of Totalism, chapter 22, for milieu control, mystical manipulation, demand for purity, confession, sacred science, loading the language, doctrine over person, and dispensing of existence.

Section Two and Section Five draw on Jennifer Freyd's work on betrayal trauma, betrayal blindness, DARVO, and institutional betrayal, and on Smith and Freyd on institutional betrayal and institutional courage.
Section Three draws on Jo Freeman, The Tyranny of Structurelessness, 1970, and Trashing: The Dark Side of Sisterhood, 1976.

Section Seven draws on the Institute for Propaganda Analysis, How to Detect Propaganda, 1937, for the seven devices, and on Christopher Paul and Miriam Matthews, The Russian Firehose of Falsehood Propaganda Model, RAND, 2016.

Learned helplessness as revised appears in Maier and Seligman, 2016. Co-rumination appears in Rose, 2002. The refusal framing behind stated boundaries appears in Patrick and Hagtvedt, Journal of Consumer Research, 2012, and the social cost of stated boundaries in Rudman and Phelan, 2008.
